title: Working in a code editor
objectives: Tell plain text from a word processor file
Name a Python file with the `.py` extension
Open a folder in VS Code and run a file from its built-in terminal

screens.prose: Ana types the same line, `print("hello")`, into two programs and saves it from each. The two files come out very different in size.
screens.question: Which file can `python3` run?

options.text: Both: they hold the same line
options.why: You judged by what you typed. The `.docx` file also stores fonts, page layout and settings, packed in a format Python cannot read.
You trusted the bigger file to hold more program. Its extra bytes are formatting, and Python cannot read them.

hints.text: Why would one line of text need nearly 12,000 bytes?
The word processor saved far more than the 14 characters she typed.
Python reads characters. Only the 15-byte file is nothing but characters.

feedback.correct: Only the editor saved exactly what she typed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what else the larger file might be storing.

explain.text: You noticed the 15-byte file is barely bigger than the line itself. The word processor wrapped the same line in fonts and layout. Python can read only the bare characters.

screens.prose: Here is `hello.py`, one byte per cell, numbered from 0. The line `print("hello")` is 14 characters long, yet the file holds 15 bytes.
screens.question: Tap the byte that you never see on the screen.

hints.text: What did Ana press after typing the closing bracket?
Look at the very end of the row.

feedback.correct: Cell 14 is the newline: the Enter key, saved as a character.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Every cell but one shows a character you can see in the line.

byKey.c6: You tapped a quote mark. You can see that one on screen.
byKey.c12: You tapped a quote mark. You can see that one on screen.
byKey.c5: You tapped the bracket. You can see that one on screen.
byKey.c13: You tapped the bracket. You can see that one on screen.

explain.text: You found the newline at the end, saved when Ana pressed Enter. A file of characters like this, and nothing else, is what Python reads. Each character here is one byte.

screens.prose: A file that holds characters and nothing else is **plain text**. A **code editor**, such as VS Code, saves plain text. The name's ending, its **extension**, tells the editor which language the text is.

state.caption: Plain text: every byte is a character

screens.question: Ana wants VS Code to colour her code as Python. What should she name the file?

options.why: You chose the extension for plain notes. The editor shows a `.txt` file as prose, with no Python colours.
You left the extension off. Then the editor cannot tell which language the file is in.
You spelled the language out. Editors look for the short form, `.py`.

hints.text: Which short ending do Python files use?
Python files end in `.py`, just as `prices.csv` ends in `.csv`.

feedback.correct: The `.py` ending tells VS Code to treat the text as Python.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Python files use a two-letter extension.

explain.text: You picked `.py`, the extension for Python. The characters inside are the same whatever the name. The extension is a label that editors use to choose colours and tools.

screens.prose:
Ana pastes her line through a word processor, then into a file. Python now refuses it:

```text
SyntaxError: invalid character '“' (U+201C)
```

state.caption: The pasted line, byte by byte

screens.question: Tap every character the word processor changed.

hints.text: The error names one character. Is there a partner to it?
The opening quote is curly. So is its partner.
Word processors turn straight quotes into curly ones. Python accepts only straight quotes.

feedback.correct: Both quotes were curled, which Python cannot read.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each quote mark with the straight `"` you typed.

byKey.one: You found the opening quote, which the error names. The closing quote was curled too; Python just stopped at the first.
byKey.brackets: You tapped the brackets. They are unchanged: the quotes inside them were curled.

explain.text: You found both curly quotes, at cells 6 and 12. A word processor "tidies" quotes as you type. A code editor never does, which is one reason to write code only in one.

screens.prose: Ana saves the same straight-quoted line as `hello.txt` instead, and runs it.
screens.question: What does the terminal print?

options.text: An error saying Python cannot run a `.txt` file
options.why: You expected Python to check the extension. It reads the characters inside, whatever the name.

options.text: Nothing: the file opens in a text editor
options.why: You pictured double-clicking the file. In the terminal, `python3` runs whatever file you name.

hints.text: Do the characters inside change when the name changes?
Python reads the plain text inside and never looks at the extension.

feedback.correct: Python ran the characters inside. The extension did not matter to it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what Python actually reads.

explain.text: You saw that Python runs a `.txt` file happily. The extension matters to people and editors, not to `python3`. We still use `.py`, so VS Code knows to help.

canvas.caption: Same 15 bytes as hello.py, so the same output: hello

screens.prose: In VS Code, Ana chooses File, then Open Folder, and picks `project`. Then she chooses Terminal, then New Terminal. A terminal opens inside the editor window.
screens.question: Tap the folder that this built-in terminal starts in.

hints.text: Which folder did she open in VS Code?
This is the folder VS Code has open.
The built-in terminal starts in the folder VS Code has open.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The built-in terminal starts in the folder VS Code has open.

byKey.a: You assumed every terminal starts at home. VS Code's built-in terminal starts in the folder it has open.
byKey.a-p-s: You went one level too deep. She opened `project`, not `src`.
byKey.a-p-h: You tapped a file. A terminal is always in a folder.

explain.text: You picked `project`, the folder VS Code has open. Its terminal starts there, so names like `hello.py` and `src/backtest.py` work as typed. That is why we open folders, not single files.

screens.prose: Next day Ana uses File, then Open File, and picks `src/backtest.py` alone. She opens the built-in terminal and runs it:

rows: python3: can't open file '/Users/ana/backtest.py': [Errno 2] No such file or directory

screens.question: Why did Python not find the file?

options.text: With no folder open, the terminal started in her home folder
The terminal looks where the open file is, and the file is locked
options.why: You expected the terminal to follow the open file. It follows the open folder, and with none open it starts at home.
A bug shows a traceback from inside the file. This message says Python never found the file at all.
Python ran: it printed this message. It simply looked in the wrong folder.

hints.text: Read the path in the message. Which folder did Python look in?
Python looked for `/Users/ana/backtest.py`. The file is in `/Users/ana/project/src`.
No folder was open, so the terminal started at home.

feedback.correct: The terminal was in `/Users/ana`, and `backtest.py` is not there.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The path in the message shows where Python looked.

byKey.follows: You assumed the terminal starts where the open file is. It starts in the open folder. With only a file open, it starts at home.

explain.text: You read the path Python tried: `/Users/ana/backtest.py`. A name you type is looked up in the terminal's folder, not the editor's file. Opening the `project` folder fixes it for good.

screens.prose: From here on, every course has you typing code. Ana types 20 words a minute while looking at the keys. After a month on keybr.com, 10 minutes a day, she types 40 without looking.
screens.question: A 300-word script takes her how many fewer minutes to type now?

hints.text: Work out each time first: words divided by words per minute.
300 ÷ 20 = 15 minutes before. Now find 300 ÷ 40.
15 − 7.5 = 7.5 minutes saved.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find both times, then subtract.

byKey.old: You gave the old time, 15 minutes. The question asks how much she saves.
byKey.speed: You subtracted the speeds, 40 − 20. That is words a minute, not minutes saved.

explain.text: You divided 300 by each speed: 15 minutes, then 7.5. Doubling speed halves the time. Touch typing also keeps your eyes on the screen, where typos show up as you make them.

screens.prose: Every run worked the same way. A file name you type is looked up inside the terminal's current folder: $$\underbrace{\texttt{/Users/ana/project}}_{\text{terminal's folder}}\;/\;\underbrace{\texttt{hello.py}}_{\text{name you typed}}$$
screens.question: VS Code has `/Users/ana/notes` open. In its terminal you type `python3 plan.py`. Which file does Python look for?

options.why: You started from home. The built-in terminal starts in the open folder, `notes`.

options.text: Whichever `plan.py` is open in the editor
options.why: You linked the run to the open file. Python only sees the name you typed and the terminal's folder.

hints.text: Where does the built-in terminal start?
Join the terminal's folder and the name with a slash.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Join the terminal's folder to the name you typed.

explain.text: You joined `notes` and `plan.py`. That join is the whole rule. When a run fails to find a file, check the folder first.

screens.prose: Ana's backtest project has a note at the top: run `python3 src/backtest.py` from the project folder. The script then reads `data/prices.csv`.
screens.question: Tap the folder she should open in VS Code so that the note works as written.

hints.text: Both `src/backtest.py` and `data/prices.csv` must make sense from the terminal's folder.
Which folder holds both `src` and `data`?
Open `project`: then `src/backtest.py` and `data/prices.csv` both exist from there.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the folder from which both paths in the note make sense.

byKey.a-p-s: You opened `src`. Then `src/backtest.py` means `src/src/backtest.py`, which does not exist.
byKey.a: You opened her home folder. From there `src/backtest.py` points nowhere: `src` is inside `project`.
byKey.a-p-d: You opened `data`. From there neither `src` nor `data` can be seen.

explain.text: You opened `project`, the folder holding both `src` and `data`. Every path in the note starts from there. Most projects expect you to work from their top folder.

ideas: Python reads plain text: the characters you typed and nothing else, which is what a code editor saves.
The extension, such as `.py`, tells people and editors what a file is; Python reads the inside, whatever the name.
Open a folder, not a file, in VS Code: its built-in terminal starts there, and names you type are looked up there.

formula.name: Where Python looks
formula.note: A file that is not found is usually a terminal in the wrong folder.

summary.trap: Opening a single file leaves the built-in terminal at home, so the file is not found.

quiz.prose: Ana has three files, each holding the same short program.
quiz.question: Which can `python3` run as it is?

options.why: You counted the code inside. The `.docx` wraps it in formatting Python cannot read.
You trusted the text on the page. A PDF stores page layout, not plain characters.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Python reads plain text only.

explain.text: A code editor saves plain text, which Python reads. Word processor files and PDFs wrap the text in formatting and layout.

quiz.prose: `total.py` holds one line, `print(2 + 2)`, and Ana pressed Enter after it.
quiz.question: How many bytes is the file?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every character, spaces and the newline included.

byKey.no-newline: You counted the twelve visible characters. Pressing Enter saved a newline too.
byKey.no-spaces: You skipped the spaces, or the newline. Spaces are characters, and so is the newline.

explain.text: `print(2 + 2)` is twelve characters, counting the two spaces. Enter adds a newline, so the file is 13 bytes.

quiz.prose: Ana's terminal prints `python3: can't open file '/Users/ana/run.py'`. Her file is `/Users/ana/project/run.py`.
quiz.question: What is the quickest fix?

options.text: Type `cd project`, then run it again

options.why: Python ran: it printed the message. It just looked in the wrong folder.
You blamed the extension. Python never found the file, whatever its name.

feedback.correct: Move the terminal to the file's folder.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare where Python looked with where the file is.

explain.text: Python looked in `/Users/ana`, but the file is in `project`. After `cd project` the same command finds it.

quiz.prose: A line copied from an email stops Python with `SyntaxError: invalid character '“' (U+201C)`.
quiz.question: What went wrong?

options.text: The quotes were curled on the way, and Python needs straight ones

options.why: You blamed `print`. It prints text fine once the quotes are straight.
You blamed the name. The problem is one character inside the file.

feedback.correct: Retype the quotes in the editor and it runs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the character the error names.

explain.text: The error names a curly quote. Email and word processors curl quotes as you type. Python accepts only the straight `"`.
